docs.text: Title: Health Education

docs.title: Important: This Is Not a Single Course
docs.text:
This project is not a single linear course written for one age group. It is a collection of health education teaching resources spanning Minnesota's proposed K-12 Health Academic Standards (2025, Commissioner Approved — see references.md and the harvest log at logs/harvest-mn-health-standards.md in the project root), organized into 8 parallel grade bands:

  • Kindergarten
  • Grade 1
  • Grade 2
  • Grade 3
  • Grade 4
  • Grade 5
  • Grades 6-8
  • Grades 9-12

Every one of the 6 content strands below runs through all 8 bands. Each band gets its own section of the site, and each section carries the full set of resource types — chapter content, quizzes, MicroSims, infographics, and references — written and calibrated for that band. A grade-3 learner and a grades-9-12 learner studying the same strand (e.g., Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) get different pages, different reading level, different MicroSim complexity, and different quiz difficulty, not the same page with a different reading age applied on the fly.

Reading level scales with band. Content generators (chapter-content- generator, quiz-generator, microsim-generator, etc.) must target band-appropriate reading level and cognitive complexity:

Band Approx. reading level Cognitive demand (per MDE anchor standards) K Pre-reader / read-aloud Identify, recognize, name 1-2 Early elementary Identify, describe, recall with simple support 3-5 Elementary Explain, identify, connect to personal experience 6-8 Middle school Analyze, evaluate influences, apply in scenarios 9-12 High school Design, evaluate, synthesize, apply across contexts

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: K-12 classroom teachers, curriculum coordinators, and students, each accessing the section that matches their grade band. Also health-standards compliance staff cross-checking site content against MDE's proposed benchmarks.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: None assumed for the Kindergarten band. Each subsequent band assumes mastery of the benchmarks in the band(s) before it, per that strand's own progression — e.g., grade 3 Food and Nutrition benchmarks assume grade 1-2 Food and Nutrition benchmarks were covered. Prerequisite edges in the learning graph should generally flow band-to-band within the same strand, not across strands.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
The 6 strands from the MDE proposed standards are the primary topic axis; each spans some or all of the 8 grade bands noted:

  1. Food and Nutrition (K-12)
  2. Human Growth and Development (K-5), continuing as Human Growth and Development and Sexual Health (6-12)
  3. Mental and Emotional Health (K-12)
  4. Personal Health and Wellness (K-12)
  5. Personal Safety and Violence Prevention (K-12)
  6. Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (6-12 only — not taught below grade 6)

Cutting across all 6 strands, the standards also define 8 anchor standards that describe the skill/knowledge type of a given benchmark (functional health knowledge, analyzing influences, accessing valid information, interpersonal communication, decision-making, goal setting, healthy practices/behaviors, promoting health/safety/wellbeing of self and others). The learning-graph-generator should treat strand × band as the concept-grouping axis and anchor standard as a tag/category on each concept, not a separate topic.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
Because outcomes scale by band, these are expressed as the progression across bands rather than a single end-state. By the end of grades 9-12, a student who has moved through all 8 bands in a strand will be able to:

  • Remember: Recall core health vocabulary and facts introduced starting in Kindergarten (e.g., food groups, emotion names, safety rules).
  • Understand: Explain why a health practice, behavior, or resource matters, in age-appropriate terms that grow more nuanced band over band.
  • Apply: Use functional health knowledge and skills (communication, decision-making, goal setting) in realistic personal and social scenarios.
  • Analyze: Evaluate influences on health behavior — media, peers, culture, advertising — with sophistication that increases from simple recognition (elementary) to critical evaluation (middle/high school).
  • Evaluate: Assess the reliability of health information, products, and services, and judge trade-offs in personal health decisions.
  • Create: Design a personal health plan, advocacy action, or peer-support strategy appropriate to the student's own life circumstances (grades 9-12 capstone-level outcome).

Content generators should produce band-scoped versions of these outcomes per section rather than assuming every learner reaches the grades 9-12 outcome.

docs.title: Course Description — Grade 1
docs.text: This is the Grade 1 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 1.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Early elementary (beginning independent readers, with read-aloud support still expected). Benchmarks shift from Kindergarten's pure identify/name toward identify and explain why, and toward simple demonstration (e.g., saying "no" to unwanted touch).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 1 students (age ~6-7) and their teachers. Short sentences, high picture-to-text ratio; independent reading is emerging but not assumed for comprehension of nuance.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Kindergarten benchmarks in the same 5 content strands (food groups, recognizing feelings, daily personal-care habits, safety rules, correct body part names) and the Kindergarten skill benchmarks (identifying trusted adults, recognizing influences, naming a personal goal).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 1 without the Kindergarten section should be briefly introduced to these ideas before Grade 1 content, since Grade 1 benchmarks build on them without re-teaching them:

  • What a food group is, and that food/water keep the body running.
  • Feelings have names, and it's healthy to talk about them.
  • A trusted adult is someone at home, school, or in the community you can ask for help.
  • Basic hygiene actions (handwashing, covering coughs) stop germs from spreading.
  • Every body part has a correct name, and your body belongs to you.
  • Simple safety rules exist at home, school, and in the community, and there are safe places to go in an emergency.

docs.text: Outcomes below are grouped by Bloom's Taxonomy level and traced to their source benchmark codes.

docs.title: 1. Remember
docs.text:
By the end of Grade 1, the student will be able to:

  1. Recall different drink types and the benefits they provide (1.1.1.2).
  2. Recall safe practices for storing, preparing, and handling food (1.1.1.4).
  3. Recall common signs that someone may be struggling emotionally (1.3.1.2).
  4. Recall the benefits of regular physical activity for health, learning, and emotions (1.4.1.2).
  5. Recall common ways germs spread (1.4.1.3).
  6. Recall safe and unsafe behaviors at home, school, and in the community (1.5.1.2).
  7. Recall different types of school emergencies (1.5.1.3).
  8. Recall the ways various influences affect health practices and behaviors (1.7.2.1).
  9. Recall when and how to seek help from others at home, school, or in the community (1.7.3.1).
  10. Recall ways to ask for help from others in making safe health-promoting choices (1.7.8.1).

docs.text:
1. Explain why eating a variety of food from all food groups is important (1.1.1.1).

  3. Describe characteristics of healthy peer relationships (1.2.1.1).

  9. Describe simple actions that prevent illness (1.4.1.3).

  11. Explain how safety drills help keep everyone safe during an emergency (1.5.1.3).
  12. Describe ways to keep one's body safe (1.5.1.4).
  13. Recognize when help is needed and who can support a health-related decision (1.7.5.1).

docs.title: 3. Apply
docs.text:
1. Demonstrate saying "no" to unwanted touch (1.5.1.4).
  2. Demonstrate communicating thoughts, feelings, wants, and needs in healthy ways (1.7.4.1).
  3. Demonstrate and track practices and behaviors that support health and wellbeing (1.7.7.1).

docs.title: 4. Analyze
docs.text:
1. Distinguish safe from unsafe behaviors at home, school, and in the community (1.5.1.2).
  2. Distinguish which people or situations positively or negatively influence a health practice or behavior (1.7.2.1).

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text: Grade 1 benchmarks do not yet include a compare-options or judge-evidence task. The closest emerging skill is recognizing when a situation calls for outside help (1.7.5.1, listed under Understand above). True evaluative reasoning (comparing choices using evidence) begins at Grade 2-3.

docs.title: 6. Create
docs.text: Grade 1 benchmarks do not yet include a design/construct task. Tracking a practiced behavior over time (1.7.7.1, listed under Apply above) is the closest precursor to the goal-design outcomes that begin at Grade 2.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 1
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 1 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 55 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 1 health benchmarks are identify-and-explain-level content for 6-7 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten band's 45-concept graph and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 1 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 24 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group, and organizes learning outcomes using the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze — with Evaluate and Create deliberately thin/absent per the developmental design of the K-12 standards, and this is explicitly documented in the text rather than an oversight).

Because this is a Grade 1 (early elementary, beginning-reader) band, the topic set is intentionally narrow — identify/explain-level content and simple demonstration tasks rather than multi-step reasoning or design tasks. This assessment therefore evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 50-55 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance.

  • Clear five-strand + Skill Standards structure maps cleanly onto a taxonomy consistent with the Kindergarten band's scheme.

  • Key Vocabulary section (14 terms) gives ready-made concept candidates.

  • Explicit "Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band" section clarifies which Kindergarten-level ideas are assumed but not re-taught.

  • Explicit, documented rationale for the thinness of Evaluate- and Create-level content avoids the false impression of an oversight and matches the developmental progression described in the standards.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No dedicated "Topics Excluded" section (partial credit given based on related context elsewhere in the document).

  • Apply and Analyze outcomes are present but modest in count, reflecting the developmental level of the band (early elementary, identify/explain plus simple demonstration) rather than a document defect.

  • Evaluate- and Create-level outcomes are explicitly deferred to Grade 2-3, which is appropriate for this band but caps rubric points under a generic scoring template designed for adult/higher-ed courses.

docs.text: This is the Grade 2 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 2.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 2 without the K-1 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Food groups exist and different foods serve different purposes; some drinks are healthier choices than others.
  • Feelings can be talked about, and different situations affect how people feel.
  • Trusted adults can be asked for help, and simple I-statements ("I feel...") are one way to share a feeling.
  • Basic hygiene habits (handwashing, covering coughs) prevent germs from spreading.
  • Technology use has safety rules, including asking permission.
  • "No" is an acceptable response to unwanted or unsafe touch, and there are known safe places and routines for school emergencies.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 2
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 2 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 55 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 2 health benchmarks are identify/describe-level content, with emerging comparison and simple cause-effect reasoning, for 7-8 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept) and Grade 1 (55-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description — Grade 3
docs.text: This is the Grade 3 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 3.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Elementary, independent readers. This band introduces the first evaluative benchmarks (e.g., "evaluate personal behaviors to prevent injuries") and the first explicit mention of puberty as a body-change topic, alongside continued describe/explain work.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 3 students (age ~8-9) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 2 benchmarks across all 5 content strands, plus the Grade 2 skill benchmarks (explaining influences, using communication skills, describing decision options, goal-setting with reflection).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 3 without the K-2 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Food groups and drink choices affect energy and growth; food safety practices exist for a reason.
  • Peer and family relationships can be healthy or unhealthy, and personal space/boundaries matter.
  • Emotions can be named, they influence behavior, and trusted adults or peers can help when someone is struggling.
  • Hygiene and environmental awareness (sun, noise, chemicals, water) protect the body; regular physical activity supports health.
  • Technology and touch both have safety rules, including saying no and knowing safe places/routines during emergencies.
  • A personal health goal can be set, acted on, and reflected on.

docs.text:

  2. Describe why it's important to limit caffeinated and sugary drinks (3.1.1.3).
  3. Describe food safety practices and preparation methods that promote healthy eating (3.1.1.4).

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 3
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 3 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 57 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 3 health benchmarks are describe/explain-level content, with the first genuine evaluate-level reasoning and the first explicit puberty topic, for 8-9 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept), Grade 1 (55-concept), and Grade 2 (55-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 3 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 27 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group, and organizes learning outcomes using the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate — with Create still deliberately thin/absent per the developmental design of the K-12 standards, explicitly documented in the text rather than an oversight).

Grade 3 is a meaningful developmental step up from Grade 2: it introduces the first genuine Evaluate-level benchmarks (evaluating personal behaviors to prevent injuries; determining validity/reliability of health information) and the first explicit mention of puberty as a body-change topic. This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 55-60 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

docs.title: Course Description — Grade 4
docs.text: This is the Grade 4 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 4.1.1.1) are <grade>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: Upper elementary. Benchmarks lean into plan, explain, analyze, and demonstrate refusal skills — the first appearance of refusal-skill language and of constructing a position from research. Per state requirements, mental health instruction becomes a required component starting at this band (2026-2027 school year, per references.md).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 4 students (age ~9-10) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 3 benchmarks across all 5 content strands, plus the Grade 3 skill benchmarks (identifying influences, judging information validity, using I-statements, setting a goal with a help/no-help decision).

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 4 without the K-3 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Nutrition labels list carbohydrates, protein, fat, and other nutrients; hydration and limiting sugary/caffeinated drinks matter.
  • Puberty is a stage of physical/emotional change that different people experience at different times, and it's normal to ask for help with it.
  • Emotions can be identified, they influence behavior, and mental health can be discussed openly with trusted adults.
  • Regular physical activity and basic hygiene/illness-prevention practices support long-term health.
  • Personal boundaries exist, sharing personal information online carries risk, and safety procedures/drills exist for real emergencies.
  • Health information should be checked for validity/reliability before it's trusted, and personal health goals can be set and pursued with or without help.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 4
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 4 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 58 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 4 health benchmarks are plan/explain/analyze-level content, with the first genuine create-level reasoning (meal planning, goal-plan development, research-based positions) and the start of required mental-health instruction, for 9-10 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept), Grade 1 (55-concept), Grade 2 (55-concept), and Grade 3 (57-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 4 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 25 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group, and organizes learning outcomes using the full 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create). This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 55-60 concepts, not the skill's generic 200-concept default, which would force invented content not grounded in the standards.

Grade 4 is a meaningful developmental step up from Grade 3: it marks the start of required mental-health instruction (per state requirements effective 2026-2027), introduces the first genuine refusal-skill language, the first explicit peer-pressure vocabulary, and — notably — the first genuine Create-level benchmarks (planning a balanced meal, developing a goal plan, constructing a research-based position), which Grade 3 explicitly deferred.

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student arriving directly at Grade 5 without the K-4 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first:

  • Nutrition labels and food groups guide meal choices; caffeinated/sugary drinks and unsafe food handling carry health risks.
  • Puberty involves physical/emotional change, and family/peer relationships influence feelings, behavior, and decisions.
  • Mental health can be supported through self-regulation and cultural practices, and it's normal and healthy to ask a trusted adult for help.
  • Bullying, exclusion, and unfair treatment harm mental health and belonging regardless of ability.
  • Regular physical activity, allergy awareness, and disease-prevention habits (hygiene, safe food/water) support long-term health.
  • Refusal skills, setting/respecting boundaries, and recognizing warning signs of unsafe situations are learnable skills, not just instincts.
  • A health-related goal can be planned with actions, resources, and known barriers, then tracked over time.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 5
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 5 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than a general-purpose graph — 70 concepts rather than 200 — because Grade 5 health benchmarks, while the richest and most granular of the K-5 bands (31 benchmark-coded topics), are still scoped to upper-elementary compare/apply/evaluate-level content for 10-11 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). Grade 5 is the last individually-graded band before the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards shift to grade spans (6-8, 9-12). It builds directly on the Kindergarten (45-concept), Grade 1 (55-concept), Grade 2 (55-concept), Grade 3 (57-concept), and Grade 4 (58-concept) bands' graphs and uses the same 7-category taxonomy for cross-band comparability.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 5 course description is a well-structured, standards-traceable document derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards. It enumerates 31 benchmark-coded topics across five content strands (Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, Personal Safety and Violence Prevention) plus a cross-cutting Skill Standards group — the richest topic set of the K-5 bands — and organizes learning outcomes using the full 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create). docs.title: Course Description — Grades 6-8
docs.text: This is the Grades 6-8 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 6.1.1.1) are <grade band>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>. This is the first band graded as a span rather than a single grade — benchmarks apply across all three grades (6, 7, 8) rather than being individually leveled.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text:
Middle school. This band introduces two entirely new elements not present in K-5:

  • Sexual Health is added to the Human Growth and Development strand (now "Human Growth and Development and Sexual Health").
  • Substance Use Awareness and Prevention appears for the first time as its own strand (not taught below grade 6). Per state requirements, cannabis/substance-use prevention curriculum is required starting the 2026-2027 school year at this band.

Cognitive demand shifts to analyze, evaluate, and design — e.g., analyzing dietary guidelines across cultures, evaluating warning signs for suicide/self-harm risk and knowing when to seek help. Note also that Appendix A of the source standards lists statewide-mandated topics that land substantially in this band: vaping awareness/prevention, cannabis/fentanyl and other substance use, and STI/HIV/HPV prevention (see references.md).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 6-8 students (age ~11-14) and their teachers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 5 benchmarks across Food and Nutrition, Human Growth and Development, Mental and Emotional Health, Personal Health and Wellness, and Personal Safety and Violence Prevention. Substance Use Awareness and Prevention has no K-5 prerequisite — it begins at this band.

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student entering directly at Grade 6-8 without the K-5 sections should be briefly introduced to these ideas first, since this band assumes them without re-teaching:

  • Reading and comparing nutrition labels; the health effects of sugary, salty, and caffeinated foods/drinks.
  • Family and peer relationships can be healthy or unhealthy; consent and coercion are different things; personal boundaries can be set and communicated.
  • Emotions influence behavior, mental health can be discussed openly, and trusted adults or professionals can help with a mental or emotional health concern — including a concern about suicide or self-harm.
  • Bullying, exclusion, and bias harm mental health and belonging; bystander actions can prevent or reduce violence.
  • Basic disease prevention (hygiene, safe food/water) and the components of physical fitness.
  • Refusal skills, boundary-setting, and recognizing warning signs of unsafe situations, both in person and online/via technology.
  • Goal-setting with a plan, resources, and known barriers, tracked and reflected on over time.

Because this band introduces Sexual Health and Substance Use for the first time, no prior-band bridging is possible for those two areas — they should be treated as genuinely new content for every student regardless of prior band completion.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Grade 6-8
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Grade 6-8 band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is substantially larger than the K-5 bands' graphs — 133 concepts, roughly double Grade 5's 70 — because Grade 6-8 is the first band graded as a 3-grade span rather than a single grade, and the first band where Sexual Health (added to Human Growth and Development) and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention (an entirely new strand) appear (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale). It builds directly on the Kindergarten through Grade 5 bands' graphs for the five strands they share, and introduces genuinely new content for Sexual Health and Substance Use Awareness, which have no true prior-band bridge.

docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Grade 6-8 course description is the most extensive and structurally mature document produced so far in this series. It is derived from the 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards and enumerates 59 benchmark-coded topics across six content strands (Food and Nutrition; Human Growth, Development, and Sexual Health; Mental and Emotional Health; Personal Health and Wellness; Personal Safety and Violence Prevention; and the entirely new Substance Use Awareness and Prevention strand) plus a large cross-cutting Skill Standards group (19 benchmarks). This assessment evaluates the description against a right-sized concept target of approximately 120-135 concepts (not the skill's generic 200-concept default), reflecting a proportional scale-up from the K-5 bands while avoiding invented content not grounded in the standards.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Every topic traces to a specific MDE benchmark code, giving the learning graph strong provenance — 59 topic benchmarks plus 19 Skill Standards benchmarks (78 total), roughly double Grade 5's 31.

  • Largest and most granular topic set of the series, reflecting the shift to a 3-grade span (6, 7, 8) rather than a single grade.

  • Explicitly documents the two structurally new elements at this band — Sexual Health folded into Human Growth and Development, and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention as a brand-new strand — with clear rationale (state mandate effective 2026-2027) and clear signaling that no K-5 bridging exists for these two areas.

  • Strongest combined Analyze/Understand tiers in the series (21 outcomes each), matching the standards' own repeated "apply skill cues to analyze" phrasing.

  • Strongest Create tier of the series (5 outcomes vs. Grade 5's 1), reflecting the band's shift toward designing workout plans, meal plans, goal plans, and health messages.

  • Detailed "Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band" section explicitly separates content that carries forward from K-5 (nutrition labels, consent/boundaries, emotions/mental health, bullying/bystander action, fitness, refusal skills, goal-setting) from content that is genuinely new at this band (Sexual Health, Substance Use).

  • Cross-references Appendix A (statewide-mandated topics: vaping, cannabis/ fentanyl, STI/HIV/HPV prevention) which land substantially in this band, strengthening traceability to the primary standards document.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• No dedicated "Topics Excluded" section (partial credit given based on related context in the Reading Level & Cognitive Demand section).

  • Remember-level outcomes are limited to 3, thinner than Understand/Analyze — but this is an accurate reflection of the standards' own emphasis on higher-order cognitive demand at this band, not a document defect.

  • Evaluate-level outcomes (2) are the thinnest Bloom's tier in this document, though Analyze-level outcomes at this band frequently blend in evaluative language ("analyze and evaluate a thoughtful decision-making process") which somewhat compensates.

docs.title: Course Description — Grades 9-12
docs.text: This is the Grades 9-12 section of the Health Education intelligent textbook. It is one of 8 parallel grade-band sections (see the site-wide Course Description); each band has its own concept list, learning graph, chapters, quizzes, MicroSims, and infographics at a matching reading level. Source: 2025 Minnesota K-12 Health Academic Standards, Commissioner Approved (see references.md). Benchmark codes below (e.g. 9.1.1.1) are <grade band>.<strand>.<anchor>.<seq>. This is the terminal band and a grade span (9-12), matching the highest cognitive demand in the standards.

docs.title: Reading Level & Cognitive Demand
docs.text: High school. Cognitive demand peaks here: design, evaluate, synthesize, apply across contexts. Benchmarks require students to construct plans (e.g., a personal nutrition plan), evaluate evidence (e.g., beverage choices using hydration/sugar/caffeine data), and reason about systemic and cultural factors (e.g., how income and food systems affect chronic-disease risk). Appendix A of the source standards lists statewide-mandated topics that culminate in this band: CPR/AED, vaping awareness/prevention, cannabis and other substance use (including fentanyl), STI/HIV/HPV prevention, and mental health education including suicide/self-harm prevention (see references.md).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Grade 9-12 students (age ~14-18) and their teachers. This is also the band most directly relevant to career/college/community readiness framing per the standards' introduction.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Grade 6-8 benchmarks across all 6 strands, including the 6-8 introduction of Sexual Health and Substance Use Awareness and Prevention.

docs.title: Bridging Concepts for Students New to This Band
docs.text:
A student entering directly at Grade 9-12 without any earlier band should be briefly introduced to these ideas first, since this band assumes them without re-teaching:

  • Reading nutrition labels and evaluating dietary guidelines across cultures; how food systems and income relate to health.
  • Relationship structures vary across individuals and cultures; consent is central to healthy relationships; STIs/HIV exist, are transmitted in known ways, and prevention/treatment resources exist.
  • Warning signs of a mental health crisis (including suicide/self-harm) can be recognized, and there are known ways to seek help for yourself or others; stigma around mental health can be actively reduced.
  • Physical fitness has multiple components; CPR/AED and basic emergency response are learnable, teachable skills.
  • Digital communication and social media carry safety, consent, and boundary implications; school-safety practices exist for emergencies.
  • Substances (alcohol, tobacco, nicotine, cannabis, and others) carry physical, mental, and legal consequences; substance-use disorder, overdose, and recovery are real, addressable situations, not just cautionary abstractions.
  • Health-related decisions and goals can be analyzed, planned, and evaluated using a structured process, not just instinct.

docs.title: Learning Graph — Kindergarten
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for the Kindergarten band of the Health Education intelligent textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this band. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the band. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

This band's graph is intentionally smaller than other bands' — 45 concepts rather than a general-purpose 200 — because Kindergarten health benchmarks are narrow, identify/name-level content for 5-6 year olds (see the Course Description Assessment for the rationale).

docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this band. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
This is the list of chapters in Health Education. Each chapter has its own folder under docs/chapters/ with a two-digit numeric prefix (for example, 01-introduction/).

Chapters are added by the book-chapter-generator skill once the learning graph is complete; their content is filled in by the chapter-content-generator skill.

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
The learning graph captures how concepts in Health Education depend on each other. It is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — every concept has a path back to one or more foundational concepts that have no prerequisites.

Once the learning-graph-generator skill runs, this section will be populated with:

  • Course Description Assessment — quality review of course-description.md
  • Concept Enumeration — the ~200 concepts the book will cover
  • Concept Taxonomy — concepts grouped into 8–12 categories
  • Graph Quality Analysis — DAG structure, foundational and terminal nodes
  • Taxonomy Distribution — concept count per taxonomy category

Use the book-installer skill (option 23) to add an interactive graph viewer once learning-graph.json exists.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).
